results.title: Impact of Label Noise on Model Generalization
results.content: In machine learning, the performance of predictive models heavily depends on the quality of the labeled data. This research explores the impact of label noise on model generalization, focusing on both supervised and semi-supervised learning settings. The study provides an in-depth analysis of how different types of label noise-random, systematic, and class-dependent-affect the training process, the robustness of models, and their ability to generalize to unseen data. The findings of this study offer guidance on how to design more resilient machine learning models and data preprocessing methods that can effectively handle label noise and improve generalization. Self-Supervised Learning for Noise Resilience: A Deep Dive into Noise-Aware Models for Robustness in Machine Learning Applications. Noise resilience is a critical challenge for machine learning models, particularly in real-world applications where noise and imperfect data are inevitable. This research explores the potential of self-supervised learning (SSL) techniques in mitigating the impact of noise on model performance. In self-supervised learning, models are trained without direct supervision by generating pseudo-labels from the input data itself. The study investigates how self-supervised learning can improve the robustness of machine learning algorithms against noise, thereby enhancing their generalization capabilities and making them more resilient in real-world, noisy environments. Model Uncertainty and Label Noise in Machine Learning: A Comprehensive Study. In the field of machine learning, the performance and reliability of predictive models heavily depend on the quality of the training data and the inherent uncertainty in model predictions. Label noise, which arises from inaccuracies in labeling due to human error, ambiguous data points, or systematic biases, poses a significant challenge in creating dependable machine learning models.

results.title: Benchmarking Label Noise in Instance Segmentation: Spatial Noise Matters
results.content: # Benchmarking Label Noise in Instance Segmentation: Spatial Noise Matters. We also propose a benchmark for weakly annotation noise, dubbed COCO-WAN, which utilizes foundation models and weak annotations to simulate semi-automated annotation tools and their noisy labels. This study sheds light on the quality of segmentation masks produced by various models and challenges the efficacy of popular methods designed to address learning with label noise. A systematic study of the effects of label noise on segmentation models can provide insights into their robustness and resilience to inaccuracies in the training regime and could enable the development and validation of new algorithms and techniques specifically designed to handle noisy labels. We tackle the challenges posed by noisy data and introduce a benchmark for assessing model robustness to label noise. We propose the Noisy Instance Segmentation Benchmarks, consisting of two datasets termed COCO-N and Cityscapes-N, each poses three levels of noise. These types of noise mirror some of the inaccuracies encountered in actual datasets and pose challenges in detecting objects, yet they cannot be adequately transferred to dense prediction tasks, where the primary focus is on high-fidelity mask annotations, which require precise and accurate labeling. By combining class noise with spatial noises, namely Scale, Localization and Approximation, we present the Noisy Instance Segmentation Benchmark for learning instance segmentation with noisy labels, namely COCO-N and Cityscapes-N, as well as an additional benchmark for weakly supervised annotation noise dubbed COCO-WAN. By incorporating both class and spatial noises, our benchmark better represents the complexities of real-world data and provides a more rigorous evaluation framework for evaluating instance segmentation models. To assess the effect of label noise, we evaluate the performance of various instance segmentation models using our newly developed benchmark. Our study defines label noise and demonstrates that instance segmentation models experience performance impairments with corrupted labels. We explore the effects of label noise on various instance segmentation models, encompassing multi-stage (Mask R-CNN [14]), single-stage (YOLACT [3]), and query-based (Mask2Former [7]) architectures. results.title: A Guide to Inter-rater Reliability and Annotator Agreement in AI
results.content: Model Agreement: How Inter-Rater Consistency Shapes Benchmark Reliability. When human annotators disagree, it raises a critical question: how can we trust an AI model trained on that data? But when human annotators disagree, the data becomes unreliable, and so do the benchmarks we use to judge model performance. Inter-rater consistency (IRC) helps measure how much human annotators agree on a task. These benchmarks use labeled data as a reference, and that is where human annotation comes in. Inter-Rater Consistency (IRC) measures the degree of agreement among different human annotators when labeling or judging the same data. Sometimes, an AI model seems to perform better than human annotators. If the benchmark was built on low inter-rater consistency, the model may only be learning to match one version of the label, not the full range of human judgment. Despite strong model performance, gold standards for coding tasks still suffer from inter-rater and annotation inconsistencies.

results.title: A Comprehensive Overview and Comparative Analysis on Deep Learning Models: CNN, RNN, LSTM, GRU - ADS
results.content: ## ADS. ## A Comprehensive Overview and Comparative Analysis on Deep Learning Models: CNN, RNN, LSTM, GRU. #### Abstract. Deep learning (DL) has emerged as a powerful subset of machine learning (ML) and artificial intelligence (AI), outperforming traditional ML methods, especially in handling unstructured and large datasets. Its impact spans across various domains, including speech recognition, healthcare, autonomous vehicles, cybersecurity, predictive analytics, and more. However, the complexity and dynamic nature of real-world problems present challenges in designing effective deep learning models. Consequently, several deep learning models have been developed to address different problems and applications. In this article, we conduct a comprehensive survey of various deep learning models, including Convolutional Neural Network (CNN), Recurrent Neural Network (RNN), Temporal Convolutional Networks (TCN), Transformer, Kolmogorov-Arnold networks (KAN), Generative Models, Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL), and Deep Transfer Learning. We examine the structure, applications, benefits, and limitations of each model. Furthermore, we perform an analysis using three publicly available datasets: IMDB, ARAS, and Fruit-360. We compared the performance of six renowned deep learning models: CNN, RNN, Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM), Bidirectional LSTM, Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU), and Bidirectional GRU alongside two newer models, TCN and Transformer, using the IMDB and ARAS datasets. Additionally, we evaluated the performance of eight CNN-based models, including VGG (Visual Geometry Group), Inception, ResNet (Residual Network), InceptionResNet, Xception (Extreme Inception), MobileNet, DenseNet (Dense Convolutional Network), and NASNet (Neural Architecture Search Network), for image classification tasks using the Fruit-360 dataset. : 10.48550/arXiv.2305.17473.
